summary: Lunar Quest is a web-based lunar landing-site navigator that helps users explore how lighting and communication conditions vary by location and date. We developed an interactive prototype that visualizes the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to selected landing sites where low-angle sunlight and rugged terrain can make mission planning challenging. The navigator also includes historic locations such as Apollo 11, Chang'e 4, and Chandrayaan-3 for broader comparison. REST and MCP tools, along with a guided AI interface, make lunar data easier to explore. By helping mission teams compare site conditions and assisting educators to understand them, Lunar Quest supports early mission planning and wider engagement with lunar exploration to the public.

Lunar Quest is an interactive web application for exploring how terrain, location, and date affect sunlight and Earth visibility on the Moon. In Compare Landing Sites, users can compare solar elevation, periods of darkness, and Earth-visibility windows across candidate sites. In Mission Simulator, users select a single site and set solar panel output and battery capacity to explore how a planned surface mission would fare through periods of darkness.

The app combines NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation data with our calculations of Sun and Earth positions. It uses the local terrain horizon to estimate when ridges or crater rims block either body. The global analysis uses a 0.25° grid derived from NASA’s global LOLA data. South-polar point queries use a 160 m grid derived from NASA’s 40 m polar elevation data. Separate first-person prototypes use 10 m LOLA terrain at the south pole and 2 m LROC NAC terrain at Apollo 11. We checked our Sun and Earth direction calculations against JPL Horizons.

We built the web application with TypeScript and Next.js, and used Three.js for interactive 3D views. REST and MCP give developers access to lunar data and comparisons, while a guided AI preview helps newcomers get started. We also used AI tools during development to assist with coding and organizing source information.

Our design connects three ways to investigate the same problem. Users can see a ridge from the surface, measure its effect on visibility, and explore what an extended period of darkness means for a simulated mission. We considered terrain resolution, date, minimum Earth elevation, and equipment assumptions because each can affect how users interpret the results. The project is intended for early site screening and education. Historical locations such as Apollo 11, Chang’e 4, and Chandrayaan-3 give learners familiar starting points for exploring those conditions.
